_l5yugYsV40.title: The Man Who Sold The Eiffel Tower
_l5yugYsV40.description: This is the unbelievable true story of Victor Lustig, the con man who sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap to Paris dealer André Poisson in 1925.
_l5yugYsV40.transcript: He leaned across the table and told the scrap metal dealers that the Eiffel Tower was coming down and that one of them was going to buy it. He said it had only ever been meant to stand for 20 years. It was rusting and the repairs were costing a fortune, so the bids were due fast. And since the public would be furious, the whole deal had to stay top secret. After the meeting, the government official, Victor Lustig, drove them out to look over the tower. And when the bids came in, Lustig told [music] one of the men, Andre Poisson, he'd won. Poisson was overjoyed. He was new to the Paris business scene. He was desperate to break into the big leagues and what could be bigger than buying the Eiffel Tower? But Poisson's wife wasn't convinced. To her, a real government deal wouldn't need to be this secret or this rushed. And so, when Lustig heard of the wife's apprehension, he confessed to being a crooked official. He told the couple that men like him were paid peanuts, but expected to live like rich men. So, if Poisson wanted this deal to go through, he'd need to slip him a little something extra. And just like that, their doubts disappeared. Because to them, a government official asking for a bribe sounded exactly [music] like the real thing. So, Poisson paid for the tower, paid the bribe on top, and within an hour, Lustig was on his way [music] to Austria with a suitcase full of cash. Because he wasn't a government official at all. He was, of course, a con man. He was sure Poisson would soon work out he'd been robbed, so he watched the Paris newspapers waiting for the police to come looking. But for weeks, there wasn't a single word. And when Lustig worked out why, it gave him another very greedy idea. See, Poisson was far too humiliated to admit he'd been tricked into buying the Eiffel Tower and he couldn't go to the police without admitting he'd bribed a government official to get it. So, Lustig thought, why not sell the tower again? Lustig went back to Paris and gave a fresh batch of scrap dealers the exact same pitch. But this time, he wasn't so lucky. Before the deal could close, one of them did what Poisson was too scared to do. He went straight to the police. Lustig suspected he'd been reported, so he fled to America. And for years, it looked like the man who'd sold the Eiffel Tower would never pay for it. But in America, still addicted to the thrill of easy money, he continued his scamming ways. This time, he started literally printing his own money. But unfortunately for Lustig, hunting down fake money was exactly what America's Secret Service had been set up to do. So, in 1935, when they finally caught him, they sent him to Alcatraz for 20 years. And when Lustig eventually died a prisoner in 1947, on his death certificate, a clerk, determined to get the last laugh on the con man, listed his occupation as apprentice salesman.

Paris, 1925. He forged government documents, led an official tour of the tower, and collected a bribe for the "right to purchase." On January 15th, in the city's north end, a 50ft tall storage tank holding over 2 million gallons of molasses suddenly burst. A 25- ft high wave of the sticky syrup surged through the streets at 35 mph, crushing buildings, overturning vehicles, and even knocking an elevated train off its tracks. The disaster claimed 21 lives and injured 150 people. Rescue efforts were hampered as workers found themselves waiting through waste deep molasses. Investigations revealed that the tank had been poorly constructed with inadequate safety testing. The company responsible, US Industrial Alcohol, faced numerous lawsuits and ultimately paid out settlements. This tragedy led to stricter building codes and regulations to ensure public safety. Remarkably, for decades after, residents claimed that on hot days, the sweet scent of molasses still lingered in the air, a haunting reminder of the day molasses turned deadly.

RaklWFblRIQ.title: This Soldier Kept Fighting for 29 Years
RaklWFblRIQ.description:
Step into the remarkable journey of Hiroo Onoda, the Japanese soldier who continued his solitary battle in the jungles of the Philippines for nearly 30 years after World War II ended. Ignorant of Japan's surrender, Onoda's unyielding dedication to his orders kept him entrenched in guerrilla warfare, surviving off the land and evading authorities. Discover the gripping tale of perseverance, duty, and the enduring impact of war.

RaklWFblRIQ.transcript: Born in 1922, Hiroo Onoda was a Japanese intelligence officer deployed to Lubang Island in the Philippines during World War II. In 1945, as the war came to a close, his commanding officers ordered him and his unit to fight to the end and not surrender under any circumstances. Despite Japan's surrender in 1945, Onoda, along with three other soldiers, continued their guerrilla warfare operations, firmly believing that the war was still ongoing. They survived by foraging in the jungle and occasionally engaging in skirmishes with local villagers and Philippine authorities. Over the years, search parties were sent to find them, and leaflets were dropped informing them that the war had ended, but they dismissed these as enemy propaganda. In 1974, his former commanding officer, Major Taniguchi, traveled to Lubang Island to personally relieve him of duty. On March 9, 1974, Hiroo Onoda emerged from the jungle to surrender.

hyaEt8EUlb8.title: He Stayed at War for 29 Years: The True Story of Hiroo Onoda #History #WWII #Japan #Onoda #TrueStory
hyaEt8EUlb8.description:
In 1945 a Japanese soldier refused to believe the war was over — Hiroo Onoda hid in Philippine jungles for 29 years, surviving on coconuts and hunted cattle, appearing skeletal and armed to locals until his former commander finally returned and read his orders aloud. He wept, lowered his rifle, and walked out of three decades lost to silence. A haunting true story of duty, isolation, and the cost of conviction.

hyaEt8EUlb8.transcript: In 1945, a Japanese soldier emerged from a Philippine jungle after the war ended. Hiroo Onoda didn't believe it. For 29 years, he'd hidden in caves, convinced the conflict continued. He rationed coconuts and hunted wild cattle. Locals saw him, pale, skeletal, armed, but he vanished into darkness. Finally, his former commander flew to the island and read his old orders aloud. Onoda wept. >> He lowered his rifle, three decades lost to silence.
